title.value: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Approach to Pneumothorax

key_points: Pneumothorax is classified as primary/secondary spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic; severity is determined by size, symptoms, and physiologic compromise.
POCUS is highly sensitive and specific for pneumothorax and should be prioritized when available; chest radiography and CT remain complementary.
Management is increasingly individualized: many stable, minimally symptomatic PSPs can be managed conservatively with robust follow‑up.
When intervention is required, needle aspiration and small‑bore tube thoracostomy are effective; ambulatory options can reduce length of stay.
Persistent air leak (PAL) requires a multidisciplinary strategy ranging from chemical/mechanical pleurodesis and VATS to autologous blood patch and endobronchial valves.
Tension pneumothorax is a life‑threatening emergency requiring immediate decompression followed by tube thoracostomy.

structures: Main bronchi and distal airways (for EBV targeting)

clinical_procedures: Point‑of‑care lung ultrasound (POCUS) for detection and confirmation of resolution
Chest radiograph (upright, supine) and computed tomography for diagnosis and characterization
Tube thoracostomy (small‑bore preferred; lateral mid‑axillary 4th–5th interspace—'triangle of safety')
Ambulatory drainage (Heimlich valve, mini‑atrium, pleural ventilation catheter)
Video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with wedge resection ± pleurodesis
Emergency needle decompression for tension pneumothorax
diagnostic_approaches: POCUS: absence of lung sliding and M‑mode 'barcode' sign; pooled sensitivity ~91% and specificity ~99% for trauma settings; superior to single‑view CXR for detection and confirming resolution.
Chest radiograph: demonstrates visceral pleural line without lung apposition; ~50 mL pleural gas visible upright; up to ~100 mL required supine.
Computed tomography: definitive test; detects occult pneumothorax and helpful in complex bullous disease or equivocal ultrasound/radiography findings.
Clinical assessment: chest pain and dyspnea most common; red flags for tension include hypotension, tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis.
treatment_algorithms: Conservative management: appropriate for stable, minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic PSP with reliable follow‑up (noninferior lung re‑expansion at 8 weeks vs intervention in an RCT).

Needle aspiration (NA): small‑bore catheter with aspiration and removal; non‑inferior to tube thoracostomy for short‑term resolution and 12‑month recurrence in meta‑analyses; shorter LOS and fewer adverse events.

Tube thoracostomy: small‑bore (≤16 Fr) preferred for spontaneous pneumothorax; similar efficacy with fewer complications and shorter LOS than large‑bore; lateral placement generally less painful than anterior approach.

Ambulatory management: Heimlich valve/mini‑atrium or pleural vent catheter allow outpatient drainage; reduces hospital days but may increase device‑related AEs; consider in carefully selected, supported patients.

Persistent air leak (PAL): typically >5–7 days of leak. Options include VATS wedge ± pleurodesis; chemical pleurodesis (graded talc) via slurry or poudrage; autologous blood patch (≈0.5–2 mL/kg or 50–100 mL); endobronchial valves (median 4–7.5 days to leak resolution).
Tension pneumothorax: immediate needle decompression followed by tube thoracostomy; mortality is high without prompt intervention.
clinical_guidelines: BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline: permits conservative management for minimally symptomatic/asymptomatic PSP regardless of size; emphasizes small‑bore tubes and lateral placement; supports ambulatory options in appropriate systems.
ACCP 2001 consensus: historically favored intervention and surgical referral for PAL after 3–5 days.
ERS 2015 task force: recommends NA as first‑line for first‑episode symptomatic PSP.
drug_information: Graded talc: common sclerosant for chemical pleurodesis; strong safety profile with larger particle sizes.
Analgesia and local anesthesia regimens for NA and tube thoracostomy per institutional protocols.

definitions.definition: Air in the pleural space occurring without trauma or known lung disease.
Pneumothorax due to underlying lung disease (e.g., COPD, ILD).
Pneumothorax resulting from blunt or penetrating chest trauma.
Pneumothorax due to medical procedures (e.g., TTNB, CVC, thoracentesis, TBLB).
Failure of pleural apposition due to airway obstruction or pleural restriction; chest tube drainage may not re‑expand lung.
Bedside ultrasound used to detect pneumothorax; high sensitivity/specificity in trauma and procedural settings.
Percutaneous pleural air evacuation using a small‑bore catheter with aspiration and removal of the catheter.
Placement of an intercostal chest drain for continuous evacuation of pleural air (small‑bore preferred for spontaneous pneumothorax).
Air leak persisting ~5–7 days after pneumothorax onset or drainage.
Minimally invasive thoracic surgery used for wedge resection and pleurodesis.
Instillation of a sclerosing agent (e.g., talc) into the pleural space to promote pleural symphysis.
Intrapleural instillation of patient’s own blood to tamponade a fistula and induce pleurodesis.
One‑way bronchial valve to reduce air leak in PAL; allows secretion egress while preventing inspiratory airflow.
Hemodynamically significant pneumothorax requiring immediate needle decompression and chest tube.

clinical_pearls: Consider conservative management for stable PSP with minimal symptoms if reliable follow‑up is feasible.
Use POCUS first where available; it outperforms single‑view CXR for detection and confirming resolution.
Prefer small‑bore chest tubes and lateral placement ('triangle of safety') when a drain is needed.
Define and document PAL consistently (e.g., Cerfolio grading); engage thoracic surgery early.
For non‑expandable lung, avoid futile chest tube drainage—address the underlying cause.

clinical_applications: Adopt an ultrasound‑first diagnostic workflow where feasible.
Integrate conservative, ambulatory, and minimally invasive strategies tailored to patient stability, preferences, and system capacity.
Standardize PAL pathways with early surgical consultation and defined criteria for chemical/mechanical pleurodesis and EBVs.
practice_recommendations: Stable PSP: consider observation with close outpatient follow‑up.
When intervening, favor NA or small‑bore chest tubes; consider ambulatory drainage for appropriate patients.
Use graded talc for chemical pleurodesis when indicated; consider ABP or EBV for PAL in non‑surgical candidates.
Immediate needle decompression for suspected tension pneumothorax.
future_directions: Randomized trials comparing pleurodesis techniques and timing for PAL.
Standardized digital air‑leak quantification and thresholds for tube removal.
Refinement of selection criteria for ambulatory management and EBV use.
controversies: Optimal first‑line intervention (NA vs chest tube) in varied health‑system contexts.
Timing and selection of pleurodesis vs surgical approaches for PAL.
Ambulatory management trade‑offs between LOS benefits and device‑related adverse events.

points: Pneumothorax management continues to evolve toward symptom‑ and physiology‑guided care with growing roles for conservative and ambulatory strategies.
POCUS enables rapid diagnosis and safer chest‑tube decision‑making; small‑bore tubes are generally preferred.
PAL requires structured, multidisciplinary pathways; VATS with adjunct pleurodesis, talc, ABP, and EBVs are key tools.
Tension pneumothorax demands immediate needle decompression and definitive drainage.
